Gap analysis and payload recommendation

RAMSES · asteroid (99942) Apophis · Objective 2. From the mission’s published objectives to a single recommended instrument, with every elimination named and sourced.

Recommendation

Gap → Required observable → Candidate instruments → Evaluation → Recommendation

A Gamma-Ray Spectrometer on the RAMSES main orbiter. The mission’s correction for space weathering would be derived from the same measurement it corrects. This supplies the external reference it lacks — no new spacecraft, no new stage, no surface asset.

Rule 1. A gap is what the mission never set out to do, not where it fell short. Rule 2. Matching ESA’s data is validation. Changing it is correction. Only the second is a contribution.

How a gap enters the register

Each objective breaks into testable measurement requirements, and every one is checked against all twelve instruments. The matrix directs attention; it never filters the check. One instrument measuring it closes the requirement. None opens a card. Confirmed cards carry forward to research, prioritisation and selection. Convergence scope is set out as a final analysis of this stage.

Method note: the card template and procedure are this project’s own, supervisor-endorsed. Every statement inside a card cites a published source.

A The four-term framework

A bare name — measure the shape — is satisfied by any camera, and exposes nothing. The step is run even where the payload plainly satisfies the requirement: what is built here is the method, not the verdict. Each requirement is constructed from four terms that make it precise and checkable.

R = f ( P , O , ε , B )

P · Purpose

One narrow scientific motive. Why does the objective want this at all?

O · Observable

The single physical quantity that serves that motive. If none exists, this is not a measurement requirement.

ε · Precision

The level that makes the measurement sufficient, not trivial. A level, never a device.

B · Boundary

A closed fence: where the requirement stops, so it never absorbs a neighbour's job.

B Requirements constructed · 19 constructed

Each card opens with its Stage A raw demand, then the constructed statement and its terms: P · O · B always, and ε only where precision decides, otherwise it lives inside the requirement without a chip of its own. ESA-derived requirements only.

No constructed requirements yet: construction proceeds objective by objective (O1 → O2 → O3 → O4).

Where this analysis converges

Fifteen requirements were constructed from ESA’s own wording across O1–O3. Checking all twelve instruments against all of them at uniform depth reproduces ESA’s trade study; the exploratory pass came back almost entirely met. This analysis converges on O2 instead, and adds SSA opportunities sharp enough to test the payload rather than restate it.

Two ways to converge were suggested:

Set aside: new objectives

Define objectives beyond ESA's. Rejected; it restructures the basis.

Adopted: converge on O2

Keep ESA's four objectives; take O2 (Composition & Interior) to full depth first, where SSA's assessment interest concentrates.

SSA opportunities

Separate from the requirements above. ESA’s O2 does not demand these; the convergence surfaced them. Only these enter the register — an uncovered margin on a requirement ESA already designed against opens a partial opening at most, never a gap. 

The eight-field card (reference)

  1. Gap ID: short unique code (GAP-1, GAP-2 …).
  2. Linked requirement: the exact requirement the gap is opened against.
  3. Parent objective: which of the objectives the requirement was derived from.
  4. Evidence: why no instrument meets it, and what the payload measures instead.
  5. Scientific impact: what the mission loses if the gap stays open.
  6. SSA strategic fit: Direct (sits in the Agency's mineralogical/resource-assessment interest), Indirect (supports it via an enabling measurement), or None.
  7. Supporting sources: the references behind the judgement (ADS-first: a clear disclosure where none exists).
  8. Gap status: Candidate → Confirmed & Selected.

Register · 4 cards

New candidate gap

GAP-1O2SSA fit: IndirectCandidate

Requirement: OPP-1: Hydration state (surface OH / H₂O band depth)

Evidence: HAMLET’s spectral range ends at 1500 nm; the diagnostic OH and water absorption bands (near 2.0 and 3.0 µm) fall outside it, and no other instrument in the payload covers the 2–3 µm region. The hydration state of the surface therefore cannot be measured at all: not even to place an upper limit.

Scientific impact: Apophis is an LL-analogue and expected to be dry, so the value here is a measured constraint rather than a resource find: Itokawa grains carried only ~683 ppm water, and whether Apophis matches that is unmeasured. Also feeds the space-weathering question (GAP-4), since solar-wind implantation is one hydration pathway.

Sources: Payload catalogue: HAMLET spectral range (Cosine RS, 650–1500 nm); Binzel et al. 2009 (2009Icar..200..480B): Apophis Sq / LL ordinary chondrite analogue

GAP-2O2SSA fit: DirectCandidate

Requirement: OPP-2: Weathering-corrected (fresh sub-surface) composition

Evidence: All compositional instruments (HAMLET, CHANCES) observe only the space-weathered surface layer. The payload has no drill, sampler, or excavation capability to expose fresh sub-surface material; the radar and SIA probe structure, not composition. Space-weathering bias therefore cannot be corrected.

Scientific impact: Remotely sensed composition may systematically misrepresent bulk composition: a bias affecting the entire resource case.

Sources: Payload catalogue: no sampler/drill in confirmed payload; space-weathering bias is a standard limitation of asteroid remote sensing

GAP-3O2SSA fit: DirectCandidate

Requirement: OPP-3: Regolith grain-size distribution

Evidence: The only instrument bearing on grain size is TIRI, via thermal inertia: a proxy that correlates with particle size but does not directly measure the distribution. Under the project’s proxy-caution rule, a proxy does not close the requirement, and no direct grain-size measurement exists in the payload.

Scientific impact: Extraction and processing feasibility depend on grain size; a thermal proxy leaves it qualitative.

Sources: Payload catalogue: TIRI (JAXA, thermal inertia / regolith properties); thermal-inertia-to-grain-size is an inferential relation, not a direct measurement

GAP-4O2SSA fit: DirectCandidate

Requirement: OPP-4: Free Fe-Ni metallic phase fraction

Evidence: MARIE (magnetometer) and HAMLET (VNIR) each give indirect indications of metal content, but neither separates free metallic Fe-Ni from iron bound in silicates or oxides. MARIE returns a bulk magnetic response; HAMLET’s VNIR slope is ambiguous for free-vs-bound metal. The specific free-metal fraction is not directly measured.

Scientific impact: Metal-extraction viability hinges on the free-metal fraction; indirect signals leave it unresolved.

Sources: Payload catalogue: MARIE (DLR, 3-axis magnetometer) and HAMLET (Cosine RS, VNIR); neither resolves free-vs-bound metal fraction directly

The register is intentionally empty at the start: cards appear only as requirements are judged against the payload.

Second convergence: from four opportunities to one

Excluding requirements corrects a logic; it does not converge. Converging is choosing one opportunity on stated criteria. The four passed through three lenses in fixed order, and a fourth test was added only because the engineering lens left two standing.

Tap any node on the map

Each lens carries its own question and its own verdict. Tap to read either.

Selected: GAP-2 — weathering-corrected composition

The only registered opportunity that is unique to the encounter, carries an unanticipated answer, and governs how every other compositional instrument is read rather than adding one isolated dataset. Apophis is classed between S and Q types, which already implies a partly refreshed surface; whether the flyby resets the weathering clock is open, and there is no second test object.

Why the gap is real: a correction with no reference

HAMLET is expected to yield a nanophase-iron maturity map. That map is derived from the same reflectance spectrum it would correct.

The gap is not a missing quantity. It is the absence of an independent reference.

Space weathering redistributes iron within the optical skin, converting silicate-bound iron to nanophase metal. It changes the optical response; it does not change bulk elemental abundance. A measurement that does not pass through reflectance is immune to the bias, and can serve as the reference the correction requires.

What the confirmed payload already covers

Overlap at the surface is not a reason to withdraw. It is the biased term of the difference, and without it there would be nothing to correct. Only one instrument makes a claim on the same ground.

The required observable

No instrument is named until the quantity is. The gap defines what must be measured; only then does the search for a candidate begin.

Quantitative elemental abundance of the near-surface regolith

Mass fractions and ratios such as Fe/Si and Mg/Si, measured over the body from orbit, by a route that does not pass through reflectance.

Why this quantity. Space weathering redistributes iron within the optical skin without removing it. Elemental abundance is therefore unchanged by the process that biases the spectrum, and can stand outside the loop as a reference. Why from orbit. The correction is applied to maps. A reference taken at one landing site cannot travel across a body; one measured on the same coverage as the spectral data can. Why below the rind. The sampling depth must exceed the layer the weathering alters, or the reference carries the same bias it is meant to correct.

Candidate instruments

Five candidates, each read the same way: what it measures and how directly that answers the gap, then whether the mission can carry it.

How five candidates became one

Two gates decided the outcome. TRL, complexity and power tied across every surviving candidate, so they appear in the trade study and not here.

A candidate is scored only until the criterion that removes it. The three that fail on architecture cannot fly on this mission, so nothing further about them bears on the decision.

Trade study: five candidates, five criteria

The observable required is quantitative elemental abundance of the near-surface regolith. Three candidates fall at the first criterion; two reach the study and separate on the second.

Out at criterion 1 — architecture

All three require physical surface interaction, which the mission architecture does not provide.

Separated at criterion 2 — complementarity

The Neutron Spectrometer ties with the GRS on every criterion but one. It measures hydrogen, not the iron that carries the bias, so it cannot constrain the mineralogical interpretation.

Where candidates tie on engineering, the observable decides.

Heritage and partnership route

Planetary gamma-ray spectroscopy is not a technology to be developed. It has flown to the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Eros, Vesta and Ceres, and is in flight to Psyche. The question is not whether the instrument can be built but through whom.

Flight heritage

MissionTarget PeriodBuilt by Why it matters here
MESSENGERMercury2004–2015APL + LLNLFirst HPGe gamma-ray spectrometer flown to a planet; the design all later units descend from.
NEAR Shoemakerasteroid Eros1996–2001APLFirst gamma-ray elemental measurement at an asteroid.
DawnVesta, Ceres2007–2018LANLElemental mapping at two small bodies from orbit.
MEGANE / MMXPhoboslaunch pendingAPL + LLNL, for JAXAThe closest precedent to this proposal: a foreign agency contributing a gamma-ray spectrometer to another agency’s small-body mission, selected under a mission-of-opportunity call with a cost cap near $20M.
Psyche GRNSasteroid Psychelaunched 2023APL + LLNL, cryocooler by Lockheed Martin ATCCurrent state of the art; measures Ni, Fe, Si, K, S, Al, Ca and the metal-to-silicate fraction. Sensor verified in flight at the 2025 Mars gravity assist.

Who builds it

OrganisationRole Record
Johns Hopkins APL
Laurel, Maryland, USA		Instrument lead and integratorBuilt the gamma-ray and neutron spectrometers for MESSENGER, NEAR, Psyche, MEGANE and Dragonfly. The single most experienced group in planetary gamma-ray spectroscopy.
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
California, USA		High-purity germanium sensorDesigned and built the HPGe sensors for MESSENGER, Psyche and MEGANE. The GeMini-Plus line is the flight-proven detector.
Los Alamos National Laboratory
New Mexico, USA		Alternative sensor routeBuilt the Dawn GRaND and Lunar Prospector instruments; the other established supplier.
Lockheed Martin ATC
California, USA		CryocoolerCryocooler. The germanium sensor must be held near −200 °C, so this is a required subsystem, not an option. Lockheed Martin ATC supplied the Psyche cooler; MEGANE and MESSENGER used a Ricor K508-series tactical cooler adapted for flight. Both are catalogue-derived units qualified by the instrument builder, so the cooler is the one part of the chain already close to off the shelf.

One route, and it is a partnership. No supplier sells a flight-ready planetary gamma-ray spectrometer, so the agreement funds a build rather than a purchase. MEGANE ran six years from selection to delivery, and that is the schedule to plan against. A catalogue detector route was examined and set aside: room-temperature CZT would remove the cooler, but it supplies a component rather than an instrument, leaving shield, electronics, structure, thermal design and qualification to the contributing agency, with no planetary flight heritage behind it. Against a launch date that does not move, that transfers work rather than saving time.

What to settle next

1 · Resolution. Confirm the achievable footprint at the planned orbit. It decides whether the output is a map or one number for the body. 2 · Accommodation. Boom or body mount. Psyche needed a boom for its precision; spacecraft materials generate the same background the instrument measures. 3 · Entry point. Approach ESA through its own instrument-selection process, and open the build conversation with APL or LANL in parallel.

Every organisation named is a US national laboratory or federally funded centre, so any agreement carries export-control and technology-transfer conditions. That is a schedule item, not an obstacle, and it belongs in the first conversation rather than the last.

Recommendation and what bounds it

A Gamma-Ray Spectrometer on the RAMSES main orbiter. It reads elements, not light, from tens of centimetres down — below the skin the weathering alters.

Main orbiter, not Farinella. The cooled sensor exceeds a 6U-XL CubeSat in mass and standing power, and the measurement needs months of accumulation. It also belongs beside HAMLET: same platform, same geometry and coverage — which is what lets one map be subtracted from the other.

The baseline does not fall short. Its weathering correction is simply drawn from the measurement it corrects, with nothing outside to check it against. This supplies that reference.

What the instrument does not do

Two properties bound it, and both describe its role. A third is a real cost: it returns elements, not minerals, so the step to an olivine-to-pyroxene ratio passes through a model. The claim narrows accordingly — it rules out the mineral models the abundances forbid. That uncertainty stands without it anyway: HAMLET ends at 1.5 µm and derives the ratio from one band alone.

Spatial resolution

Reads a broad patch, tens to hundreds of metres.

Defines the role

The mission already maps in detail. This gives the value that map is read against.

Integration time

Gamma emission is faint; precision takes hours and days of counts.

Defines the role

It is passive — no laser, no mechanism, no pointing. It gathers while the spacecraft works.

Coupled geochemical and mineralogical analysis

The GRS adds an independent elemental constraint to HAMLET’s mineralogy. Together they narrow the interpretation, while elements and minerals stay linked through inversion models.

Without the 2 µm pyroxene band the inversion leans on shorter wavelengths, and carries the uncertainty that follows. Elemental abundances reduce it; they do not remove it. The limit is the spectral range, not the instrument.

Scope of the measurement

It measures bulk elements over large footprints, complementing rather than replacing hyperspectral mapping, and its precision follows cumulative observation time. Neither is a shortfall: no one instrument delivers spatial detail and independent geochemistry at once.

Open item: the footprint and observation time achievable at the planned altitude.

Conclusion: how the instrument can be obtained

Ask APL and Lawrence Livermore for a copy of an instrument they have already built. For this opportunity, on this mission, that is the only option that works.

The answer takes weeks. The science does not change either way.

RAMSES mission, overview

Reference document for ongoing RAMSES research

Where this phase sits

Following the selection of RAMSES as the reference mission, this phase conducts an internal gap investigation to identify scientific measurement opportunities where an additional national payload could maximise the mission’s scientific return. The objective is not to identify deficiencies in the baseline mission, but to determine where a complementary contribution would provide the greatest added value.

1. Mission identity

RAMSES (Rapid Apophis Mission for SpacE Safety) is a joint ESA–JAXA planetary defence mission, executed under ESA leadership, with prime contractor OHB Italia. The mission was formally selected and funded at ESA's Ministerial Council meeting in Bremen in late November 2025, bringing total contract value to approximately €150 million.

Lead agency

ESA (with JAXA)

Prime contractor

OHB Italia

Mission type

Planetary defence

Spacecraft heritage

Based on ESA's Hera mission

2. Mission purpose & objectives

RAMSES will rendezvous with near-Earth asteroid (99942) Apophis and study it before, during, and after its exceptionally close Earth flyby, assessing how the asteroid's shape, surface, orbit, rotation, and orientation respond to Earth's tidal forces.

  • Conduct a before-and-after survey of Apophis' shape, surface, orbit, rotation, and orientation.
  • Determine asteroid composition, interior structure, cohesion, mass, density, and porosity.
  • Support planetary defence by improving understanding of how to deflect a hazardous asteroid.
  • Provide scientific insight into the formation and evolution of the Solar System, since asteroids are time capsules over four billion years old.

3. Target: asteroid Apophis

Designation

(99942) Apophis

Size

~375 metres across

Close approach date

13 April 2029

Flyby distance

~32,000 km from Earth

This distance is about one-tenth of the way to the Moon and closer than satellites in geosynchronous orbit. While there is no risk of impact, the encounter is an extraordinarily rare scientific opportunity.

4. Key dates & timeline

Selection / funding

November 2025 (ESA Ministerial Council)

Launch window

Spring 2028, H3 rocket, Tanegashima

Arrival at Apophis

February 2029

Close Earth flyby

13 April 2029

RAMSES shares its launch with JAXA's DESTINY+ mission. DESTINY+ will perform a flyby of Apophis ahead of RAMSES' arrival, capturing the first space images of the asteroid in preparation for RAMSES.

5. Spacecraft & payload (summary)

RAMSES is derived from ESA's Hera spacecraft design, adapted for a direct transfer trajectory to Apophis. It carries a main orbiter payload plus two deployable 6U-XL CubeSats. Full instrument-level detail is covered in the separate RAMSES Payload Overview reference; this section summarises the structure only.

5.1 Main orbiter payload

AFC (×2)

Navigation & wide-field imaging

CHANCES

High-res colour surface imaging

HAMLET

Hyperspectral mineral mapping

TIRI

Thermal infrared imaging (JAXA)

RSE

Mass, gravity, tidal deformation

RPS

Plasma / charged-particle environment

5.2 CubeSats

Farinella (orbiter)

HORUS imager, low-frequency radar, VISTA dust analyser

Don Quijote (lander)

SIA seismometer, gravimeter, MARIE magnetometer

6. International partners & industry

  • ESA: mission leadership, spacecraft design, integration, and operations.
  • JAXA: solar arrays, TIRI thermal imager, H3 rocket launch (rideshare with DESTINY+).
  • OHB Italia: prime contractor for the RAMSES spacecraft.
  • University of Bern, CHANCES camera.
  • Cosine Italia: HAMLET hyperspectral camera.
  • Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research: RPS plasma spectrometer.
  • DLR / German National Space Programme, MARIE magnetometer.
  • Tyvak International (Italy), Farinella CubeSat.
  • Emxys (Spain) & GomSpace (Denmark): Don Quijote lander CubeSat.
  • ISAE-SUPAERO / CNES (France): SIA seismic instrument.

7. Strategic & scientific significance

  • Planetary defence: improves understanding of how asteroids respond to external forces, informing future deflection strategies.
  • Unique timing: Apophis' 2029 flyby is a non-repeatable natural experiment: no comparable close approach is expected again soon.
  • Heritage continuity: builds directly on ESA's Hera mission and JAXA's Hayabusa missions, reinforcing an established ESA–JAXA partnership.
  • Solar System science: asteroid composition and structure data informs models of planetary formation and evolution.

RAMSES mission, payload overview

Confirmed payload, finalised at ESA's November 2025 Ministerial Council: with detailed instrument research and objective-traceability matrix

Baseline frozen: analysis anchored to the confirmed 12-instrument payload as catalogued in Stage 1 (July 2026). Later payload changes do not invalidate this baseline; they trigger a dated revision.

1. Main orbiter payloads

AFC (×2)

Asteroid Framing Cameras

Wide field-of-view navigation and science cameras used to capture the whole asteroid at relatively low resolution, supporting both spacecraft navigation and imaging.

CHANCES

Colour High-resolution Apophis Narrow-angle CamEra System

High-resolution colour imager that captures surface reflectance at different wavelengths to study Apophis' physical properties and mineralogical composition, and to record subtle surface changes caused by the Earth flyby.

HAMLET

HyperScout for Apophis Multispectral Exploration and Taxonomy

Hyperspectral camera covering two spectral channels (650–960 nm and 960–1500 nm) for detailed surface characterisation, mapping mineral and elemental composition, physical properties, and space-weathering effects.

TIRI

Thermal Infrared Imager

JAXA-provided thermal infrared camera (Hera heritage) that measures surface temperature to characterise thermal inertia and physical properties of the asteroid's regolith.

RSE

Radio Science Experiment

Uses Earth-based radiometric tracking, optical imaging, and inter-satellite links to measure Apophis' mass, gravity field, and tidal deformation during the close encounter.

RPS

RAMSES Plasma Spectrometer

Measures the energy and distribution of ions and electrons surrounding the spacecraft and asteroid surface material, studying the thin cloud of charged particles around Apophis.

2. CubeSat payloads

Farinella (orbiter CubeSat)

HORUS

Optical imaging instrument

Dual-purpose high-resolution scientific imager and navigation camera, capturing close-up imagery from Farinella's low-altitude orbit around Apophis.

Low-frequency radar

 

Probes the asteroid's internal structure, helping determine subsurface composition, density variation, and cohesion.

VISTA

Dust analyser (Milani heritage)

Characterises dust and particles ejected from or surrounding the asteroid during the close encounter.

Don Quijote (lander CubeSat)

SIA

Seismic Instrument for Asteroids

Deployed to the surface to measure asteroid seismicity from tidal forces, plus other sources such as micro-meteoroid impacts or thermal cracking: the first in-situ seismic study of an asteroid surface.

Gravimeter

 

Measures local gravitational acceleration at the surface to help characterise Apophis' internal mass distribution and density.

MARIE

Magnetosphere-induced Apophis Response Investigation Experiment

Surface magnetometer studying how Apophis responds as it passes through Earth's magnetosphere during the close flyby, measuring possible surface magnetisation.

3. Detailed Instrument Research

Independent research per confirmed instrument. The "Likely gap theme" tag is a preliminary science-area indicator only: formal gap classification is pending the project's Stage 2 analysis and may differ once that work is complete.

AFC (×2): Asteroid Framing Cameras

Core payload, main orbiter

ManufacturerJena-Optronik (subsidiary of Jenoptik), Germany
CharacteristicsBroad field-of-view monochrome cameras; carried over from Hera's design; complements CHANCES' higher resolution by capturing the whole asteroid at low resolution.
Likely gap themeWide-field imaging / navigation

CHANCES

Colour High-resolution Apophis Narrow-angle CamEra System

ManufacturerUniversity of Bern, Space Research & Planetary Sciences Division, Switzerland
CharacteristicsHigh-resolution multi-wavelength imager; builds on heritage from CoCA (Comet Interceptor) and CaSSIS (ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter); selected as an ESA "payload of opportunity" in April 2025.
Likely gap themeSurface morphology & change detection

HAMLET

HyperScout for Apophis Multispectral Exploration and Taxonomy

ManufacturerCosine Remote Sensing, Italy/Netherlands-origin hyperspectral heritage line
CharacteristicsHyperspectral imager spanning two channels (650–960 nm, 960–1500 nm); selected by ESA alongside CHANCES in March 2025 as a new opportunity payload for mineralogical/compositional mapping.
Likely gap themeMineralogy & compositional mapping

TIRI

Thermal Infrared Imager

ManufacturerJAXA, Japan
CharacteristicsThermal infrared camera carrying direct heritage from Hera; maps temperature distribution to estimate thermal inertia and regolith physical properties.
Likely gap themeThermal / regolith properties

RSE

Radio Science Experiment

ManufacturerESA-led, core payload (multi-national, no single national lead)
CharacteristicsCombines Earth-based radiometric tracking, optical navigation data, and inter-satellite links between RAMSES and the two CubeSats to derive mass, gravity field, spin, and small-scale tidal deformation.
Likely gap themeMass, gravity & tidal response

RPS

RAMSES Plasma Spectrometer

ManufacturerMax Planck Institute for Solar System Research, Göttingen, Germany
CharacteristicsHigh-resolution spectrometer for charged particles; built from a spare model of the JEI sensor on ESA's JUICE mission; first asteroid mission to fly an instrument of this type, possibly able to detect lifted dust.
Likely gap themePlasma / space-weathering environment

HORUS (Farinella CubeSat)

Optical imaging instrument

ManufacturerTyvak International and Politecnico di Milano, Italy
CharacteristicsDual-purpose high-resolution science imager and navigation camera, operating from Farinella's low-altitude orbit for close-up imagery unattainable from the main orbiter.
Likely gap themeClose-range / low-altitude imaging

Low-frequency radar (Farinella CubeSat)

Internal structure probing instrument

ManufacturerGrenoble Institute of Planetology and Astrophysics (IPAG/UGA), France
CharacteristicsRadar heritage from the Hera mission; complements the SIA seismometer to probe internal heterogeneity, density variation, and cohesion at meter-scale resolution.
Likely gap themeSubsurface / internal structure

VISTA (Farinella CubeSat)

Dust analyser

ManufacturerItaly (heritage from the Milani CubeSat, Hera mission family)
CharacteristicsCharacterises particles ejected from or surrounding the asteroid; reused instrument design rather than a newly built unit for RAMSES.
Likely gap themeDust / ejecta environment

SIA (Don Quijote CubeSat)

Seismic Instrument for Asteroids

ManufacturerISAE-SUPAERO (SSPA team, DEOS department), with CNES support and IPGP collaboration, France
CharacteristicsFirst seismometer ever deployed on a near-Earth asteroid; records tidally-induced seismicity plus micro-meteoroid impacts and thermal cracking from the surface.
Likely gap themeSeismic / interior geophysics

Gravimeter (Don Quijote CubeSat)

 

ManufacturerPart of the Don Quijote CubeSat consortium (Europe); independent manufacturer not separately confirmed in public sources
CharacteristicsMeasures local gravitational acceleration at the landing site, contributing to density and internal mass-distribution estimates alongside RSE and the radar.
Likely gap themeDensity & mass distribution

MARIE (Don Quijote CubeSat)

Magnetosphere-induced Apophis Response Investigation Experiment

ManufacturerDLR (German Aerospace Center), funded almost exclusively through Germany's National Space Programme
CharacteristicsThree-axis coil magnetometer; an early in-space test of miniaturised magnetometer technology developed under Germany's 2023 space strategy; measures possible surface magnetisation during approach and landing.
Likely gap themeMagnetic field / magnetosphere interaction

4. Core Mission Objectives

  • O1: Shape, orbit & rotation tracking: before/after survey of Apophis' shape, surface, orbit, rotation, and orientation.
  • O2: Composition & interior structure: determine composition, interior structure, cohesion, mass, density, and porosity.
  • O3: Planetary defence / tidal response: assess how the asteroid responds to Earth's tidal forces, informing deflection strategy.
  • O4: Solar System science: insight into Solar System formation and evolution from asteroid material.

5. Instrument-to-Objective Matrix

How to read this matrix. Rows are the 12 confirmed instruments; columns are the four mission objectives as published by ESA. Each cell answers exactly one question: does this instrument provide at least one measurement that serves this objective? True means yes: hover (or tap) the cell to see which measurement. False means no contribution was identified: hover to see why. The matrix is a hypothesis generator: it sets where the Stage 2 gap analysis looks first. It does not declare gaps.

6. Matrix Insights

  • Reading the totals (post supervisor re-check): O3 (planetary defence / tidal) and O4 (Solar System science) are now the strongest columns at 11 of 12 each, followed by O2 (composition & interior) with 8 and O1 (shape / orbit / rotation) with 4: exactly what a payload built around the 2029 tidal encounter should look like.
  • O4 was re-assessed with a direct criterion set by the supervisors: does the instrument help, in one way or another, in knowing the asteroid's historical evolution? A direct yes → True; otherwise False. Under this criterion 11 of 12 instruments qualify, since nearly every measured property of the body (shape, composition, interior, surface state, magnetisation) is a record of its history. The finer instrument-by-instrument discrimination moves to requirement level in Stage 2, where it belongs.
  • RPS is the single exception on O4: and now the payload's only single-objective specialist (O3): it measures the present-day charged-particle environment around the asteroid rather than a property of the body itself, so it carries no record of the asteroid's historical evolution. CHANCES and RSE are True on all four objectives.
  • A False is a lead, not yet a gap. Every False cell is carried into the Stage 2 requirement-level mapping, where it either closes with evidence or enters the candidate gap register. Of the three conservative calls flagged in Stage 1, two (TIRI×O3, Radar×O4) were closed as True in the supervisor re-check round; HORUS×O3 remains open for Stage 2.

The four objectives are as published by ESA for the Ramses mission (before-and-after survey of shape, surface, orbit, rotation and orientation; composition, interior structure, cohesion, mass, density and porosity; response to Earth's tidal forces for planetary defence; and Solar System science).
